Exp8 unwinders: early and late, fast and slow

How an MM gets out of inventory it absorbed. Section 4.4 splits the 25,705 absorbers that accumulated inventory into early and late unwinders against the price extreme. Sections 10 to 12 read the resting orders of shocked MMs, how fast the population recovers, and how MMs quote while they unwind. Sections 4.4 and 12 are on the taker-imbalance events; sections 10 and 11 are on wallet inventory shocks.

Key results

After the peak the accumulating-side quote moves away and the unwind-side quote barely moves§10.2 →The book reacts within 9 minutes at the median and is refilled within 30 minutes in 87% of shocks§10.4 →Half of the shocks have 60% of the excursion back within 30 minutes; 11.9% never do within six hours§11.3 →Exit-side quoting orders recovery speed across MMs, not shock by shock§11.4 →While at least 75% of the position is still on, fast unwinders lean toward the exit§12.3 →Faster unwinders lean more, between MMs and hardly within one (older test)§12.4 →

Section, table and figure numbers are those of the single Exp8 record, so they do not start at 1 here. Definitions shared by every section are in the notation and event-set sections of the main page.

Each finding shows its headline. Click one to read the explanation.

4.4 Early and late unwinders among absorbers that accumulated inventory

Section 4.4 of the Exp8 record. Its population, the event window and the active rule are defined in §4.1 on the main page.

Timing is measured only on MMs whose inventory actually grew on the absorption side during the event. 25,705 of the 126,846 event × active-MM rows clear that bar, a median 23 per event, and they hold 64% of all hit-side maker USD. Early means half of the accumulation was already gone when the price reached its extreme.

Which MMs the timing split is measured on, how early and late are decided, and what each row of the table measures

Symbols used in this section

  • MM is a market maker: a wallet the MM label model calls a HYPE market maker on that date. An active MM also has at least one post-only fill in the two hours before the event and at least one fill during it (§4.1). One row is one event × active MM.
  • t0 and t1 are the start and end of the event window [t0,t1): 30 minutes for 75% of events, at most 180 minutes. PRE2H is the two hours ending at t0.
  • Absorption side is the maker side that fills the surging takers. s=+1 when takers sell, so absorbing them makes the MM longer, and s=−1 when takers buy.
  • qt is the MM's HYPE position at the end of the 1-minute bin ending at t. xt=s (qt−qt0) is the inventory built since the window start, positive toward the absorption side.
  • A, the accumulation, is the largest xt over the window's minutes: the most inventory the event built, counted from the position at t0. t*, the inventory peak, is the first minute where xt reaches A.
  • L, the level at the inventory peak, is L=s (qt*−median6h q), with the median over the six hours before t0: how far the peak position sits from the MM's normal position.
  • sig24, the MM's own scale, is sig24=max[1.4826 MAD(q−median6hq), 0.02 p95|q|, 12500/mid] in HYPE, every term over the 24 hours before the event. The first term is the typical distance of the position from its six-hour median, measured robustly. The other two are floors: 2% of the 95th-percentile absolute position, and $12,500 of HYPE. It is one number per MM per event.
  • Shocked means |dq|≥3 sig24, where dq=qt1−qt0 is the window's end-minus-start position change.

How A and L differ

A and L are compared with the same sig24. They differ only in the starting position. A counts from the position at t0. L counts from the six-hour median. The two disagree when the MM starts the window away from its median. Take an MM with sig24=1,000 HYPE on an event where takers sell (s=+1):

  • It starts 2,000 HYPE short of its median and buys 2,000 HYPE. Then A is 2 sig24 but L is 0: the event only brought it back to normal.
  • It starts 2,000 HYPE long of its median and buys 500 HYPE. Then L is 2.5 sig24 but A is 0.5 sig24: it was already long before the event.

Which MMs are in the population

An absorber that accumulated inventory is an active MM in one event with all three of

  • A≥sig24: the event built at least one sig24 of inventory;
  • L≥sig24: the peak position is at least one sig24 on the absorption side of the six-hour median;
  • the fill condition: absorption-side maker fills larger than all opposite-side fills over [t0,t*), in HYPE, so the inventory came from filling takers and not from the MM's own crossing orders.

The shock rule needs |dq|≥3 sig24 on the end-minus-start change. This rule needs 1 sig24 at the inventory peak. 5,857 of the 25,705 admitted rows are also shocked.

How early and late are decided

The price extreme text is the minute of the highest 1-minute mid over [t0,t1+30 min) when the event's price move is up, and of the lowest when it is down. The share of the accumulation already given back at that minute is

G=1−xtextA

read at the end of the extreme minute. G is a share of A, not a cutoff: 0% means the MM still holds all of A, 50% means half of it is gone, 100% means the position is back at its window-start level, above 100% means it went past that level, and a negative value means the MM held more than A. A row is early when t*≤text and G≥0.5, and late otherwise. Late has two shapes: held more than half when the peak is at or before the extreme and G is under 0.5, and peak after the price extreme when the wallet was still building after the price had turned. Early and late partition the population, and G is on the table as a continuous measure beside them.

The 30-minute extension matters because the price extreme of 22% of events falls on the last minute of the window, which is a truncation rather than a turn; with the extension the extreme falls after the window in 58% of events and on the last minute in 4.7%. Measuring text inside the window alone gives 3,877 early, 14,683 late-held and 7,145 late-peak rows, and 91.1% of rows keep the same label under both.

What each row of the table measures

  • Given back at the price extreme is G; given back at the event end is the same ratio evaluated at t1. Both are negative when the wallet held more than A at that minute.
  • ACC, the accumulation phase, is [t0,t*): from the window start to the MM's own inventory peak. Its length is the inventory peak minute row of Table 12, so two MMs in one event have ACC phases of different lengths.
  • UNW, the unwind phase, is [t*,t*+2 h): always two hours after the inventory peak, whether or not the position is already gone. An early MM is back to half of A a median 3 minutes after its peak, so most of its UNW fills are ordinary two-sided quoting after the unwind.
  • t* is searched only inside the event window [t0,t1). The window is the net-flow box that defines the event, so A counts inventory built while the event's taker flow ran. An MM still building at t1 gets its peak on the window's last minute (16.8% of rows). Table 16 lets the peak come up to 120 minutes after t1.
  • Taker share is crossing fill USD over all fill USD, inside the event window and inside UNW.
  • Submits / PRE2H divides the phase's submissions per minute on one side by the same wallet's submissions per minute on the same side over PRE2H. The absorption side and the opposite side are kept apart because the two move in opposite directions during an unwind.
  • Maker M30 and M60 are markouts of the phase's maker fills at 30 and 60 minutes, in bps. One fill of size q HYPE at price p with mid m 30 minutes later marks out d (m−p) q dollars, with d=+1 for a buy and −1 for a sell. The row value sums these over the phase's maker fills and divides by the same fills' USD volume. Positive means the price moved in the MM's favour.
  • Markout rows pool both sides unless the row names a side. Absorption-side fills add to the event's inventory. Exit-side fills reduce it.
  • Minutes to half counts from the inventory peak t* to the first minute with xt≤A/2. The search runs for 360 minutes after t*.
  • Censored at 360 means the MM never got down to half of A within those 360 minutes. The row is recorded as 360, so a quantile cell of 360 is the cap and not a measured time. Read p25 and p50, not the mean. The row share censored at 360 min of Table 12 gives the share at the cap, and Table 14 shows what the censored rows did after the window.
  • UNW best-level distance is the distance from the mid to the nearest resting order on that side, in bps, median over the UNW minutes with an order there. UNW resting size averages every UNW minute, zero-quote minutes included.

Column key and source
All 914 events, 126,846 event × active-MM rows, 2025-10-10 included. A (accumulation) is the most inventory the event built, counted from the MM's position at the window start t0. L (level at the inventory peak) is the peak position counted from the MM's median position over the six hours before t0. Both are in HYPE and positive toward the absorption side, the maker side that fills the surging takers. Both are compared with the same sig24, the MM's own position scale over the 24 hours before the event (§4.4). Every row also requires the fill condition: absorption-side maker fills larger than all opposite-side fills between t0 and the inventory peak. rows = event × MM rows admitted; per event = median over events of the number admitted; also shocked and not shocked split the admitted rows by |dq|≥3 sig24, with dq the window's end-minus-start position change; hit-side maker USD, pooled = admitted rows' maker USD on the side the takers hit, over all active MMs' maker USD on that side, summed over events; per-event median = the same share computed per event, then the median; start 1 sig24 on the opposite side = share of admitted rows whose position at t0 was already at least one sig24 on the opposite side of the six-hour median. The bold row is the rule used in the rest of this section. Source tables/review0915_unwind_absorber_variants.csv, which also carries the 2025-10-10-excluded sample, 0.5 and 2 sig24 versions of every rule, and the rule without the fill condition.
  • A≥sig24 and L≥sig24 remove different MMs, so the rule requires both.
    A≥sig24 alone admits 31,406 rows. 19.9% of them started the window at least one sig24 on the opposite side of their six-hour median, so absorbing the takers moved them back toward their normal position. L≥sig24 alone admits 35,330 rows. Some of them were already far from their median before the window and built little inside it: their median A is 1.72 sig24, against 2.33 sig24 under the rule used here.
  • 1 sig24 is the threshold that keeps most of the absorption while keeping the measured quantity meaningful.
    Requiring both at 0.5 sig24 admits 38,114 rows holding 74% of hit-side maker USD. At 1 sig24, 25,705 rows hold 64%. At 2 sig24, 13,312 rows hold 45%. At 0.5 sig24 an MM at the $12,500 floor is admitted with $6,250 of inventory, too small for "gave back half" to mean anything.
  • The rule selects the wallets that carry the event, and the shock rule is not what selects them.
    65% of each event's five biggest absorbers accumulate inventory by this rule, against 23.6% flagged by the shock rule (§8.2). 5,857 of the 25,705 admitted rows are shocked, and 1,635 of the 7,492 shocked wallet-events are outside it: 872 of those ended the window with the position moved against the absorption side, and 536 had A≥sig24 but L< sig24.

Column key and source
  • Cells list p5, p25, p50 (bold), p75 and p95 over wallet-events. Rows with a single number are shares of the column.
  • Sample. All 914 events, 2025-10-10 included; the rows fall on 912 of them. Columns: early (5,340 rows); late (20,365), the union of the last two columns; late, held more than half (16,510); late, peak after the price extreme (3,855).
  • Inventory. x is the inventory built since the window start t0, positive toward the absorption side, the maker side that fills the surging takers. A (accumulation) is the largest x inside the event window [t0,t1), and the inventory peak t* is the first minute x reaches it. Minute rows count from t0.
  • Price extreme. The highest 1-minute mid (price up) or lowest (price down) over [t0,t1+30 min).
  • Given back = 1−x/A at that minute. 0% holds all of A, 50% has shed half, 100% is back at the window-start position, and a negative value holds more than A.
  • Classes. Early: peak at or before the price extreme and at least 50% given back there. Late, held more than half: peak at or before the extreme and under 50% given back. Late, peak after the price extreme: peak after it.
  • Phases. PRE2H = [t0−2 h,t0); ACC (accumulation) = [t0,t*); UNW (unwind) = [t*,t*+2 h), always two hours.
  • Taker share is crossing fill USD over all fill USD, inside [t0,t1) (event) or UNW (unwind).
  • Submits / PRE2H is the phase's submits per minute on that side over the same wallet's PRE2H rate on that side. Rows with no PRE2H submits on that side are dropped.
  • Maker M30, M60 are the USD-weighted markouts of the phase's maker fills at 30 and 60 minutes, in bps (basis points, 0.01%), positive when the price moved in the MM's favour. Rows that name no side pool both sides. Absorption side keeps the fills that add to the inventory, exit side the fills that reduce it. A wallet-event with no maker fill on that side has no value on that row.
  • ACC exit-side share of maker USD
    is exit-side maker USD over all maker USD in ACC. UNW maker USD / A is all UNW maker USD over A valued at the mid at the peak.
  • Minutes to half runs from t* to the first minute with x≤A/2, searched for 360 minutes. A wallet-event that never gets there is censored and recorded as 360, so a cell of 360 is the cap.
  • Quotes. Best-level distance is bps from the mid, median over UNW minutes with a resting order on that side. Resting size averages every UNW minute, zero minutes included. Both come from the raw order store and cover 5,278 early and 17,868 late rows for distance, and 4,232 and 15,635 for submits.
  • Source tables/review0915_unwind_early_vs_late.csv, built by code/review0915_unwind_build.py, review0915_unwind_orders.py and review0915_unwind_reduce.py. Side rows and the two volume rows: tables/review0917_side_markouts.csv, built by code/review0917_unwind_horizon_build.py and review0917_unwind_horizon_reduce.py; they reproduce the pooled rows exactly.
  • One absorber in five is early.
    5,340 of 25,705 rows (20.8%) have given back half of the accumulation by the price extreme, 16,510 (64.2%) are still holding more than half, and 3,855 (15.0%) had not yet reached their own peak when the price turned. Excluding 2025-10-10 leaves 5,306 early rows of 25,561.
  • The two groups are separated by timing and not by size.
    Median accumulation is $55.5k for early rows and $51.6k for late rows, 2.50 against 2.29 sig24.
  • Early unwinders are back to half within 3 minutes of their inventory peak; late unwinders take 96 minutes.
    No early row is censored at six hours against 29.5% of late rows, and the late p75 is the 360-minute cap itself. Censored rows are mostly MMs whose inventory kept growing after the window, not events that kept going (Table 14, Table 15).
  • The fills that reduce the position lose money in every class. The positive UNW markout comes from absorption-side fills.
    UNW exit-side M30 is −0.7 bps for early rows, −3.8 for held more than half and −5.8 for peak after the extreme. UNW absorption-side fills, which add inventory back after the turn, mark out +9.8, +20.8 and +23.7 bps.
  • Pooled over both sides, late rows mark out better in UNW.
    UNW maker M30 is +4.2 bps against +2.2 for early rows and M60 is +4.4 against +1.9 (Mann-Whitney p < 1e−8 on both). Within the 837 events that produce both kinds the median gap is +2.0 bps in the same direction, and late is ahead in 58.7% of them.
  • A one-sided markout mostly follows the price path, so compare it with PRE2H and not with zero.
    The side split already shows before the event. Over PRE2H, late rows' absorption-side maker fills mark out −27.3 bps at 30 minutes and their exit-side fills +35.6 bps, because the price then moves in the event's direction.
  • Accumulation costs early and late rows about the same.
    ACC maker M30 is −15.3 bps for early rows and −13.6 for late rows, so the price runs against the inventory while it is being built either way.
  • Only the peak-after column marks out positive in ACC, because its peaks come after the price has turned.
    Its ACC M30 is +19.8 bps, and its absorption-side fills +23.6 bps, against −43.6 for held more than half. The sign follows the peak's position against the price extreme in every class (Table 13; the split by class is in its source table).
  • Early rows' UNW is mostly ordinary quoting after the unwind.
    Their UNW maker USD is 10.1 times A, against 1.9 for held more than half and 1.1 for peak after the extreme. 28.0% of early rows' ACC maker USD is already on the exit side at the median, against 5.8% for held more than half.
  • Neither group crosses the spread to get out.
    The median unwind taker share is zero in both, and the p75 is 12.1% for early rows against 18.0% for late rows.
  • What separates the two books is where the quotes sit and how much size stands on each side.
    In UNW the late rows' nearest absorption-side order is 9.1 bps from the mid against 8.2 bps on the opposite side, and their absorption-side resting size is 92 HYPE against 128 on the opposite side. Early rows quote closer and symmetrically, 5.8 against 5.4 bps and 352 against 353 HYPE.
  • The message rate is ordinary in both groups.
    UNW submits are 1.16 times the wallet's own PRE2H rate on the absorption side for early rows and 1.01 for late rows.
  • Two thirds of early rows are brief accumulations.
    65.4% give back half within five minutes of their inventory peak, against 10.8% of late rows. Requiring the accumulation to stand for five consecutive minutes leaves 2,349 early rows of 21,056, 11.2% instead of 20.8%.
Why the accumulation markout changes sign, what the censored rows are, and what changes when the peak may come after the window

Symbols used in these tables

  • t0 and t1 are the start and end of the event window; x is the inventory built since t0, positive toward the absorption side; A is its largest value inside the window and t*, the inventory peak, the first minute it gets there.
  • The price extreme is the highest (price up) or lowest (price down) 1-minute mid over [t0,t1+30 min). Early, late, held more than half and late, peak after the price extreme are the classes of Table 12.
  • ACC = [t0,t*), UNW = [t*,t*+2 h). Maker M30 is the USD-weighted 30-minute markout of the phase's maker fills in bps, positive when the price moved in the MM's favour. Absorption-side fills add to the inventory, exit-side fills reduce it.
  • Hit-side taker flow is taker USD per minute on the side the event's takers hit (sells for a sell event). Censored means the inventory never came down to half of A within 360 minutes of t*.

Column key and source
  • Columns: how far after t1 the peak search may reach. 0 is the in-window peak of Table 12. For a later search the peak is the first minute of the largest x over [t0,t1+H), and ACC and UNW move with it.
  • Price extreme: over [t0,t1+30 min) for 0 and +30, and over [t0,t1+H) for +60 and +120. Classes follow the rule of Table 12 on that peak and that extreme.
  • Censored at 240 min
    and minutes to half use one 240-minute search for every column, because the stored inventory path ends 390 minutes after t1. With 360 minutes the 0 column gives 23.4%.

    : the inventory at the later peak over A. Same 25,705 rows in every column; all 914 events, 2025-10-10 included.
  • Source tables/review0917_horizon_classes.csv (also absorption-side markouts and pooled UNW), built by code/review0917_unwind_horizon_build.py and review0917_unwind_horizon_reduce.py.
  • Letting the peak come 30 minutes later moves 38.6% of peaks and doubles the peak-after class.
    Late, peak after the price extreme goes from 15.0% to 30.5% of rows, taken from held more than half (64.2% to 49.3%). Early is 20.1% at +30 and 25.4% at +120, where the price extreme also moves later.
  • Censoring barely changes. 28.1% of rows are censored at 240 minutes with the in-window peak, and 24.7% with a peak up to 120 minutes later.
  • The ACC markout gap narrows but keeps its sign.
    The peak-after median goes from +19.8 bps to +4.0 at +30, and held more than half from −23.2 to −14.8.
  • Exit-side UNW fills lose money in both late classes at every horizon.
    Held more than half goes from −3.8 to −11.2 bps, and peak after the extreme from −5.8 to −10.4.
  • Table 12 and the rest of this section keep the in-window peak.
    The flow after t1 is still 2.88 times the PRE2H median minute, so a later horizon is defensible too, and the choice is open.

Order skew by timing class

Before the event and over the 2 hours after the inventory peak, the median gap between an MM’s exit-side and absorption-side quotes is under 0.5 bps in every class. The classes differ in the first minutes after the peak. Over the first 5 minutes the early class quotes its best exit-side order 4.34 bps nearer the touch than its best absorption-side order, the late, held more than half class 1.63 bps nearer, and the late, peak after the price extreme class 0.26 bps farther (class medians). The gap comes mainly from the absorption side: after the peak its best quote sits farther from the touch and its resting size is smaller, while the exit side moves little.

Symbols used here

  • Population. The 25,705 absorbers that accumulated inventory (event × MM rows, all 914 events, 2025-10-10 included), split into the three classes of this section. early: t* ≤ text and G ≥ 0.5 (5,340 rows). late, held more than half: t* ≤ text and G < 0.5 (16,510 rows). late, peak after the price extreme: t* > text (3,855 rows). The text shortens the two late names to late held and late peak-after. text is the minute of the price extreme over the event window plus 30 minutes, and G is the share of the accumulation A already given back at that minute.
  • t0 is the clock time at which the event window starts. t* is the MM’s own inventory peak: the end of the first minute at which the inventory built since t0 reaches its maximum A. Two MMs in the same event have different t*.
  • Absorption side is the side of the MM’s quotes that fills the surging takers: the bid when takers sell, the ask when takers buy. Exit side is the other side, whose fills reduce the inventory the event built.
  • Touch is the best price of the whole book on the same side as the order: the best bid for a bid, the best ask for an ask, read as the last book state before the minute. The distance of a bid at price p is 104 (best bid − p) / mid bps, and of an ask 104 (p − best ask) / mid bps. Zero means at the touch.
  • Three measures, one sign: exit minus absorption.
    Δbest = Dbest(exit) − Dbest(absorption)    Δvw = Dvw(exit) − Dvw(absorption)    Δsize = Q(exit) − Q(absorption)Dbest is the distance of the MM’s nearest resting order on that side to the touch. Dvw is the size-weighted mean distance of all its resting orders on that side. Q is its resting size on that side in HYPE. A negative Δbest or Δvw means the exit side sits nearer the touch. A positive Δsize means more size rests on the exit side. The exit share of resting size, Q(exit) / [Q(exit) + Q(absorption)], is the same comparison without the MM’s scale; 0.5 is a balanced book.
  • Window values. Orders are read on 1-minute snapshots. Over a window, Dbest is the median over the minutes with an order on that side, Dvw is weighted over all order-minutes, and Q is the mean per minute with empty minutes counted as zero.
  • Windows, in clock order. PRE2H = [t0 − 2 h, t0); ACC = [t0, t*); M5 = [t*, t* + 5 min); M15 = [t*, t* + 15 min); UNW = [t*, t* + 2 h). M5 lies inside M15, and M15 inside UNW. H60 = [t*, t* + min(T60, 120) min) ends when the MM has given back 60% of A, so its length depends on the MM: a median 4 minutes for early rows, 96 for late held and 120 for late peak-after.
  • Change from PRE2H is a window’s value minus the same MM’s value in PRE2H of the same event. It removes the differences in book scale between classes.

Book size differs by class: the median early row rests 367.5 HYPE on the exit side before the event, the median late held row 151.5 and the median late peak-after row 37.9. Table 21 therefore states each window as a change from the same MM’s PRE2H value, and the findings below quote those changes.

  • The earlier a class unwinds, the harder it leans its best quotes toward the exit right after its peak: 4.10 bps for early, 2.00 bps for late held and 0.38 bps for late peak-after, in the first 5 minutes.
    These are medians of M5 minus the same MM’s PRE2H value, on 3,560, 10,031 and 2,115 rows. 80.0% of early rows move toward the exit, against 63.1% and 52.5%. The size-weighted distance moves the same way by less: −2.30, −1.03 and −0.88 bps (Table 21).
  • MMs that unwind late already quote the exit side farther from the touch while they accumulate: +1.04 bps for late held and +2.21 bps for late peak-after, against −0.53 bps for early.
    As changes from PRE2H the three numbers are +0.55, +1.21 and −0.44 bps, on 12,753, 2,546 and 4,350 rows. The exit side carries the change: its best quote moves +0.52 bps (late held) and +0.80 bps (late peak-after) from PRE2H to ACC, while the absorption-side best quote moves 0.00 and −0.02 bps (Table 23). A distance grows both when the touch moves away from a resting order and when the MM moves the order, and the measure combines the two.
  • Resting size tells the same story as price: in the 5 minutes after the peak the early class rests 41.9 HYPE more on the exit side than before the event, late held 9.9 HYPE and late peak-after 0.1 HYPE.
    The exit share of resting size in M5 is 0.556, 0.511 and 0.500 at the median, from 0.500, 0.497 and 0.495 in PRE2H. Over UNW the share is 0.502, 0.503 and 0.499. Both sides contribute for the early class: the median row’s absorption-side size changes by −23.6 HYPE and its exit-side size by +9.9 HYPE. For late held rows the absorption side changes by −8.8 HYPE and the exit side by 0.0 HYPE (Table 19 and Table 23).

Remarks that need attention. Two readings of the same tables that are not findings yet: each is a number without an explanation that the timing class accounts for.

  • Over the 2 hours after the peak the early class shows 0.00 bps of change, and the two late classes keep 0.80 and 0.68 bps toward the exit.
    Over the first 15 minutes the changes are −1.72, −1.46 and −0.78 bps. Among shocked MMs the early median difference is −7.61 bps at the peak minute, −4.61 at +5, −2.51 at +15, −1.33 at +30 and −0.73 at +60 minutes (n = 287 to 333 wallet-events). The late held median is −1.55 bps at the peak minute, −2.21 at +5 and −1.08 at +60 (Figure 9, Table 24). Needs attention: the late classes still hold inventory at two hours and the early class does not, so the remaining lean may only restate the class. Settled by the lean at equal shares of the position still held.
  • The gap after the peak comes from the absorption side: from PRE2H to M5 the median early row’s absorption-side best quote moves 2.62 bps away from the touch, and its exit-side best quote moves 0.55 bps toward it.
    For late held rows the absorption side moves +1.60 bps and the exit side +0.05 bps; for late peak-after rows +0.30 and +0.12 bps (Table 23; n = 3,767, 11,191 and 2,523 rows on the absorption side). In levels the median early absorption-side best distance is 4.23 bps in PRE2H and 9.43 bps in M5, and the exit-side one 4.16 and 3.68 bps (Table 22). Net absorption-side fills end at the peak by construction. Orders consumed by those fills and orders the MM canceled both leave the absorption side farther from the touch, and the 1-minute snapshots combine the two. Needs attention: this split cannot tell a quote the MM pulled from a quote the surge consumed. Settled by the order stream: cancels against fills on the absorption side, from the peak to five minutes after it.

Limits

  • The measures are descriptive. The touch moves during the event, so a distance can change while the MM’s order stays at the same price.
  • Figure 9 and Figure 10 cover the shocked rows only, 5,857 of 25,705 (22.8%): 528 early, 4,250 late held and 1,079 late peak-after wallet-events. On the window measures the shocked early and late held rows move more than their class and the shocked late peak-after rows move less: the median M5 change of the best-quote difference is −5.23, −2.43 and +0.21 bps on shocked rows, against −4.10, −2.00 and −0.38 bps on all rows.
  • A distance difference needs a resting order on both sides. In M5 that holds for 67.6% of early, 63.3% of late held and 57.7% of late peak-after rows; rows quoting one side only enter the size panels alone.
  • M5, M15 and H60 exist for 25,081 of the 25,705 rows. The other 624 rows have no post-only fill in PRE2H and were left out of the short-window build.
  • The order store is complete (at least 90% of post-only fill orders found) on the dates of 73.7% of early, 72.8% of late held and 67.5% of late peak-after rows. On those dates alone the median change of either distance difference, in any window and class, differs from the all-date value by at most 0.29 bps.
  • The early label uses the outcome: an early row has given back half of A by the price extreme, and its median T60 is 4 minutes. M5 therefore covers most of an early unwind and the first minutes of a late one, and H60 compares windows of 4 and 96 minutes.
  • Quotes are read at the minute instant. 23.6% of early, 28.0% of late held and 41.5% of late peak-after wallet-minutes have nothing resting at that instant and enter no minute-grain size measure.

10. What a shocked roster MM does to its own resting orders

Event set 4: all 181 roster wallet shocks. Windows are anchored on form_start and the peak bin, read as 5-minute bin labels, which puts every window five minutes early (§15).

After the inventory peak the shocked MM moves its accumulating-side best quote away from the market and leaves its unwind-side quote almost where it was. Resting size stays close to balanced, both sides are cancelled and reposted faster, and the quote asymmetry is mostly gone within two hours.

Population and grain
  • Population. All 181 shocks of Exp8's frozen roster catalogue, on 9 of the roster ten: MM01 53, MM02 46, MM05 25, MM03 18, MM07 16, MM04 9, MM09 8, MM10 4, MM08 2. 125 up and 56 down; 125 revert, 32 step, 24 partial; 60 ALONE, 64 FEW, 56 BROAD, 1 unclassified. Only the shocked wallet is read. Exp9 names wallets by roster rank, and rank rk is MM0k here.
  • Grain. The wallet's resting orders rebuilt from the raw HYPE order stream and valued at every minute-end from 24 hours before the build to 6 hours after the peak. 930,121,285 order events (posts, cancels, fills) are stored. A resting order is an ALO or GTC limit order the exchange accepted; rejected orders never rested and are excluded.
  • Clock. Windows are anchored on the catalogue's 5-minute bin labels, the convention the data notes flag as five minutes early.

10.1 Definitions

Sides, distances, depth skew, imbalances, windows, reaction latency
  • SAME and OPP. SAME is the side whose fills built the position: the bid after an up shock, the ask after a down shock. OPP is the other side, the one whose fills unwind it. Every paired measure is signed so that a positive value leans toward getting out, which lets up and down shocks pool.
  • Distance to the market's best. For a resting order at price p, with mid m and the market's best price b on the same side (last book state at or before the minute-end), dbid=104×b−pm,  dask=104×p−bm. 0 is at the market's best, positive is behind it, negative improves on it. dSAME and dOPP are the distances of the wallet's own best quote on each side. The distance from mid uses m in place of b.
  • Quote asymmetry. A=dSAME−dOPP in bps, per minute. Positive means the side that built the position is quoted further from the market.
  • Depth skew. With Q the resting notional in USD on a side, K=QOPP−QSAMEQOPP+QSAME.
  • Distance buckets. Touch: d≤0. Near: 0<d≤10 bps. Mid: 10<d≤100 bps. Far: d>100 bps. HYPE's tick is $0.001, which is 0.25 bps at $40.
  • Post and cancel imbalance in bucket b. With Pb the USD posted in the bucket in the minute, ΠPb = PbOPP−PbSAMEPbOPP+PbSAME. ΠCb is the same on cancelled USD. Both are undefined in a minute with no flow in the bucket.
  • Withdrawal rate and fill-through. w=Ct/Qt−1, cancelled USD in the minute over resting USD at the previous minute-end, per side. φSAME is the same ratio on maker-filled USD. Order lifetime at cancel is the median age of the orders cancelled in the minute.
  • Windows. PRE = [form_start − 2 h, form_start), the reference. FORM = [form_start, peak]. PEAK = peak ± 2 min. POST1 = (peak, peak + 30 min]. POST2 = (peak + 30 min, peak + 2 h]. TAIL = (peak + 2 h, peak + 6 h]. BASE = [form_start − 24 h, form_start − 2 h), active minutes only.
  • Statistic. Per shock, the median of a 1-minute measure over the window's minutes. Tables show the median of those per-shock values across shocks. A change is the per-shock paired difference against the same shock's PRE, and its share is the share of shocks with the predicted sign (a prediction of ≥ 0 counts zeros).
  • Reaction latency L (seconds). From the taker-surge onset, the first minute in [form_start − 15 min, peak] with hit-side taker USD at least 3 times its BASE median, to the first minute with QSAME≤0.5 times its onset value or dSAME at least 10 bps wider than at onset. Refill: the first minute after the peak with QSAME at 80% or more of its BASE median.

10.4 The book reacts within 9 minutes at the median and is refilled within 30 minutes in 87% of shocks

  • The taker surge starts before the build.
    The 3-times rule finds an onset in 175 of 181 shocks, a median 13 minutes before form_start.
  • Latency p5 / p25 / p50 / p75 / p95 is 1 / 3 / 9 / 23 / 61 minutes
    (60 / 180 / 540 / 1,380 / 3,648 s) over the 165 shocks with SAME depth at onset. None is censored at 6 hours. The depth rule fires first in 110 shocks and the 10 bps widening in 55.
  • Up and down shocks react at similar speed.
    Median 8 minutes for 117 up shocks and 11.5 minutes for 48 down shocks, p25 3 minutes for both.
  • SAME depth comes back.
    It is at 80% or more of its BASE median by +30 minutes in 152 of 174 shocks (87%), by +2 hours in 94% and by +6 hours in 95%.
  • Latency does not scale with shock size.
    Responses of 1 minute and of over 100 minutes span the same range of peak deviations, and the per-wallet slopes run from −1.93 to +0.48 with no common sign.

10.6 Limits

What this does not establish
  • 181 shocks on 9 wallets, 99 of them on MM01 and MM02. Many share a date and a market move, so shares describe this set and Wilcoxon p-values overstate certainty.
  • Distances use a book state 0.27 s stale at the median and up to 16 s at p99 on the worst date, so orders near the 0 and 10 bps bucket edges can switch buckets.
  • The −0.19 bps OPP change is one tick or less at HYPE's prices. It is not an improvement of the unwind-side quote.
  • The cancel imbalance does not measure withdrawal for MMs that cancel within seconds; the per-side withdrawal rate is the substitute.
  • Peer MMs in each window (median 7) are stored but not read. Unwind speed and markouts are not measured here.
  • Only the notional-weighted share within 10 bps of the touch describes the shape of the resting orders; the size-weighted mean distance and the distance to the best filled price were not built.
  • Exp10's rebuild of 2025-08-11 found an order-feed gap. Exp9's three shocks of episode 39 (MM01, MM02, MM04) carry 438 orders with no terminal row that the build kept resting; they have not been re-read.

11. Population shocks: how fast MMs recover, and what quote skew says about it

Event set 5: 812 population wallet shocks on 88 of 148 MMs. Recovery times run from the peak bin, on clock time. The skew tests read resting orders inside the set-1 boxes: 468 shocks whose peak falls near an event or control window, and 7,492 shocked wallet-events.

Exp8's frozen shock detector finds 812 shocks on 88 of the 148 population MMs, and the median shock has 60% of its excursion back 30 minutes after the peak. MMs that put more of their orders on the exit side are the MMs that recover fast, but inside one MM the same skew explains almost nothing.

Population and grain
  • Population. The 148 wallets with at least 10 active HYPE days, 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30. Roster wallets are MM01 to MM10; the others are coded P###.
  • Grain. Each wallet's exchange-reported end-of-bin HYPE position on a contiguous 5-minute grid over its active days (4.48 million bins). Inactive days are missing, so no window crosses them. Fills and order submits per bin and side come from hype_mm_5m and hype_mm_5m_orders_ext.
  • Clock. form_start and peak are 5-minute bin labels; the clock time is the label plus 5 minutes, and the skew matching below uses clock time.
  • Quote data. The skew tests read the resting-order state of the population event study (the 915 market taker-imbalance events of the population section), because resting orders are built per event window.

11.1 Definitions

Detector, MM gates, recovery times, classes, skew measures, samples
  • Detector. Exp8's frozen v2 detector run unchanged: a candidate run of bins with |z| ≥ 6 on an active day, a start observed within 3 h, peak deviation times mid of at least $100k, 60% of the build inside one 25-minute span, a directed build, prominence of at least 1.5 over the 3 h before (and after, except for steps), and Exp8's activity gate. The trailing scale is Exp8's rule rebuilt on this grid: scale=max(1.4826×MAD7d, 0.02×p9530d|q|, 12500/mid) with the MAD taken around the trailing 6-hour median over the wallet's active bins in the trailing 7 days.
  • Actively market making. Gate 1: at least one fill in each of the two hours before form_start. Gate 2: at least one bid submit and one ask submit in those two hours.
  • Excursion and recovery times. With m the median position over the 24 bins before form_start and s=±1 the shock direction, e(t)=s×(q(t)−m) and E is e at the peak. T50, T60, T75 and T100 are the minutes after the peak until e(t)≤0.5E, 0.4E, 0.25E and 0; censored at 360 minutes.
  • Recovery classes. Fast: T60≤30 min. Medium: 30<T60≤120. Slow or held: T60>120 or censored. The cuts align with Exp9's POST1 window and the 2-hour unwind window of the skew measures.
  • Skew measures, per shocked wallet-event and window, signed to the wallet's own exit side. Exit-side submit share: share of order submits on the side that reduces the position (0.5 is balanced). Size skew: resting HYPE on the exit side minus the accumulating side. Best-quote distance skew: exit-side best quote distance from mid minus the accumulating side's, positive when the exit quote is further away. Windows: PRE2H (2 h before the event), ACC (event start to the wallet's own peak) and UNW (own peak to +2 h).
  • Minutes to half (min_to_half). Minutes after the event end until half the wallet's excursion is back, on a 1-minute grid, censored at 360.
  • Samples. Sample (a): the 468 of the 812 shocks whose peak falls inside or within 30 minutes of an event or control window; 298 of them have a wallet-event row. Sample (b): every shocked wallet-event (|zdq| ≥ 3) in an event window, 7,492 rows on 642 wallets. Within demeans both variables inside wallets with at least 10 rows; across MMs correlates wallet medians over those 181 wallets.

11.2 812 shocks on 88 of 148 MMs, 5.2 per wallet per 100 active days

  • Prominence is the largest single cut.
    5,586 candidates; 5,183 anchored; 4,304 above $100k; 3,280 sudden; 3,026 directed; 1,240 prominent (1,786 removed, most inside a longer swing); 887 active; 812 after merging overlapping windows.
  • The MM gates remove one shock.
    Gate 1 removes none and gate 2 removes a wallet quoting one side only, leaving 811.
  • The roster shocks a little more often than the rest.
    The roster ten have 200 shocks on 3,198 active days (6.3 per 100); the other 138 wallets have 612 on 12,367 days (4.9 per 100).
  • Shocks concentrate on a minority of wallets.
    60 of the 148 wallets have no shock, 36 have one or two shocks, 31 have three to nine and 21 have ten or more, from 4.9 (P077) to 55.6 (P005) per 100 active days. MM02 is at 17.0 and MM01 at 11.6.
  • Direction and class. 472 up and 340 down; 536 revert, 184 step and 92 partial.
  • A velocity gate finds a superset.
    Replacing the 60% suddenness rule by the v3 rule of at least 3 trailing-scale units per 30 minutes gives 1,151 shocks, including all 812. The extra 339 are large slow builds.

  • Shock frequency does not order recovery speed.

Sample (b), 7,492 shocked wallet-events on 642 wallets; n varies because a distance needs a quote on both sides. A negative ρ means more lean toward the exit goes with faster recovery; for the distance skew the same reading is a positive ρ. Pooled: over wallet-events. Within: both variables demeaned inside wallets with at least 10 rows. Per wallet: median of the per-wallet ρ, with the share of wallets whose ρ is negative. Across MMs: ρ of wallet medians over the 181 wallets. Terciles: median minutes to half in the low, middle and high third of the measure. Bold marks |ρ| of at least 0.34. Source Exp9/tables/pop_skew_vs_recovery.csv, pop_skew_vs_recovery_cross_wallet.csv, pop_skew_vs_recovery_by_wallet.csv; sample (a) in pop_skew_vs_recovery_sample_a.csv.
  • The relation lives between MMs.
    A wallet's median exit-side submit share during the build orders its median recovery time with ρ = −0.48 over 181 wallets, and in the unwind window with −0.49. By tercile of the build-window share, median minutes to half is 360 (share 0.001, 67% censored), 174 and 95 (share 0.50, 23% censored).
  • Inside a MM the skew explains little.
    Demeaned within wallet, the build-window submit share keeps ρ = −0.09 (n = 4,594) and the size skews are at zero.
  • The pooled −0.34 is mostly one-sided quoting.
    1,179 wallet-events (21.7%) post under 10% of their submits on the exit side during the build; their median minutes to half is 360, with 67.5% censored. The 3,677 rows with a share of 0.3 or more have a median of 74 minutes, and among them ρ = −0.07.
  • Shock size does not carry it.
    In terciles of the peak excursion in own scale units (medians 3.5, 4.8 and 8.2), the build-window submit-share ρ is −0.31, −0.33 and −0.37.
  • MMs that quote wider recover slower.
    The build-window distance skew has ρ = +0.38 across MMs, and the exit-side best distance itself has pooled ρ = +0.25 (n = 5,096).
  • Sample (a) adds nothing.
    With 136 to 298 shocks on 18 to 24 wallets, every pooled ρ is inside ±0.20 except the build-window distance skew (+0.19, n = 136, p = 0.03).
What this does not establish
  • 344 of the 812 population shocks (217 dates, 64 wallets) fall outside every event and control window and have no quote data, so the skew results rest on shocks inside market events.
  • The across-MM relation is descriptive. Book size, quoting width and one- or two-sided presence differ between wallets at the same time, and the exit-side submit share is correlated with all three.
  • Minutes to half runs from the event end and T60 from the wallet's own peak; the unwind skew window and the recovery clock overlap in time. A fast unwind shortens the part of the window with a reason to skew, which would push the sign positive; the observed sign is negative.
  • The detector re-detects 166 of the 181 Exp8 catalogue shocks on the same wallet in the same peak hour (167 within ±1 h) and finds 34 roster shocks outside the catalogue. The 14 unreproduced and 34 extra roster shocks come from the position series (exchange-reported against Exp8's fill-anchored panel), so population counts that mix the two series disagree at the 5 to 10% level.
  • Controls are left out of the skew tests because their exit side is arbitrary; re-signing them by the wallet's own position change gives the same signs. The v3 catalogue is not carried through recovery or skew.

12. How MMs quote while they unwind, by recovery speed

Event set 1: 7,492 shocked wallet-events inside 856 of the 915 net-flow boxes, 7,404 on 851 events after excluding 2025-10-10. t0 is the box start, the own peak is the wallet's largest excursion inside the box, and UNW is the two hours after it.

Averaged over the two hours after its own peak, the median shocked MM does not lean its resting orders toward the exit. Fast unwinders do lean, but only while most of the position is still on: 60% of resting size on the exit side and the exit quote 3.3 bps nearer the touch. Faster unwinders lean more across MMs and hardly within one.

Population and grain
  • Population. Every shocked wallet-event (|zdq| ≥ 3) of the population event study in an event window: 7,492 rows on 642 wallets, 856 events, 340 dates. The quantiles and tests exclude 2025-10-10 (7,404 rows, 640 wallets, 851 events).
  • Grain. Resting orders per minute and side, rebuilt from the raw order store with the population study's lifecycle rule (an order rests from placement to its cancel or fill, partial fills reduce it, right-censored orders dropped). 4.14 million minute rows; 120 unwind-window minutes per wallet-event.

12.1 Definitions

Exit and accumulating sides, windows, share still held, tilt, recovery class
  • Exit and accumulating sides. The exit side is the side whose fills reduce the position built in the event: the ask for a wallet whose position rose over the event, the bid otherwise. The accumulating side built it. This is SAME and OPP relabelled to the wallet's own position.
  • Windows. PRE2H = [t0 − 2 h, t0); ACC = [t0, own peak); UNW = [own peak, own peak + 2 h), with t0 the event start and the own peak the minute of the wallet's largest excursion inside the event.
  • Share still held. Each UNW minute is grouped by the wallet's excursion as a share of its peak excursion: 100–75%, 75–50%, 50–25%, 25–0%.
  • Distance to the touch. The wallet's best quote on a side against the market's best same-side price at that minute (last book state at or before; median staleness 0.1 s), in bps of mid; 0 is at the touch, positive behind it.
  • Exit-side shares. Exit-side share of resting size = mean exit-side resting HYPE over the mean of both sides, minutes without an order counting as zero. Exit-side share of submits is the same on order submits.
  • Tilt. tilt=dacc−dexit with each d the median over the window's minutes of the best quote's distance to the touch. Positive means the exit quote is closer to the touch. The size-weighted version uses the size-weighted mean distance of all resting orders.
  • Recovery class from minutes to half (after the event end, 1-minute grid, censored at 360): fast ≤ 30 minutes, medium 30 to 120, slow above 120 or censored.

  • The lean is a state, not a window.
    Fast rows put 60% of resting size and 59% of submits on the exit side and quote it 3.3 bps nearer the touch while at least three quarters of the excursion is held. They spend a median 15 minutes there. Under a quarter held, the book is level and the tilt is −0.3 bps.
  • For fast rows the lean is a change from their own habit.
    In the 100–75% state the exit-side size share exceeds the same wallet-event's PRE2H share by a median 0.12 for fast rows (77% positive), 0.04 for medium (72%) and 0.00 for slow (54%).
  • Slow rows stay in the first state and quote level.
    The median slow row spends all 120 minutes with more than 75% still held, at 50% of size and submits on each side and no tilt.
  • During the build slow rows lean the other way.
    In ACC their exit-side submit share is 0.35 and the tilt −3.6 bps; fast rows are level (0.49, 0.0 bps). The population section finds the same pre-event lean toward the side that later fills the MM.

  • Every measure orders speed across MMs and barely within one.
    Across MMs |ρ| is 0.16 to 0.50; within a wallet it is under 0.12. The mid-based submit-share test of the previous section gave the same split (−0.48 across, −0.09 within).
  • Among two-sided quoters only the distance gradient survives.
    On the 4,079 rows with both sides present in at least half the unwind minutes, the size share is 0.50 in every class (pooled ρ = −0.03). The exit best quote sits 5.2, 6.4 and 11.0 bps from the touch for fast, medium and slow (pooled ρ = +0.37).
  • Distance to the best maker fill agrees.
    The exit quote's distance to the minute's best same-side maker fill price has pooled ρ = +0.25 and across-MM ρ = +0.51.
What this does not establish
  • Whether the lean causes the fast unwind. A wallet with 60% of its size on the exit side is filled there more often by construction, and a hedge on another venue or coin would produce the same HYPE path with no lean.
  • 68% of slow rows are censored at 360 minutes, so their ordering against uncensored slow rows carries no information.
  • The touch is the last book state at or before the minute; a quote posted inside the spread in that minute shows a negative distance, and the wallet's own order can be the touch.
  • 20 of 4.14 million minute rows lack a book state. Book staleness is 0.1 s at p50, 2.0 s at p95 and 3.9 s at p99.
  • Touch distances use the ts_bbo mid at the minute instant and mid-based columns the median trade mid of the minute; only the mid-based family is checked against the population table.
  • 2025-10-10 is excluded from every quantile and test here, and the source tables hold no all-dates version.

12.5 Fast and slow unwinders among the MMs that accumulated inventory

Event set 1: 35,612 event × MM rows on all 914 net-flow boxes, 2025-10-10 included. 6,236 of the rows are shocked MMs, on 820 events. Every window after the peak starts at t*, the MM’s own inventory peak, so two MMs in the same event have different clocks.

Fast unwinders lean their quotes toward the exit more than slow unwinders do, but only for the few minutes they still hold the position. While they hold it, the fast MMs move their quote skew +4.41 bps toward the exit, against +0.56 bps for the slow MMs. Averaged over the two hours after the peak the fast MMs show +0.00 bps, which is what the earlier version of this section reported. Nobody crosses the spread to get out. Speed comes from volume: in the two hours after the peak a fast MM fills 8.0 times its accumulation on the exit side and 6.6 times on the absorption side, and the position leaves as the difference. A slow MM fills about 0.5 times its accumulation on each side.

What changed from the 2026-09-16 version.
  • Population. The earlier version used the 25,705 rows of the own-sigma rule. This version uses the 35,612 rows that pass the own-sigma rule or the population rule among active MMs, and reports the shocked MMs separately.
  • “Fast MMs do not tilt at all”
    holds only for the two-hour average. Over the minutes they still hold the position, fast MMs lean the most (Table 68).
  • “Inside an MM, more tilt goes with a slower unwind”
    also came from the two-hour window. Over the first 5 minutes after the peak, faster MMs lean more, mostly between MMs (ρ −0.53 across MMs, −0.04 inside an MM) (Table 71).
  • Unchanged. The exit-side taker share is 0 at the median in every class. Exit-side fills after the peak lose money for the fast and middle classes.
  • Dropped here. The early and late labels of §4.4. Early is almost entirely the fast class measured against the price clock, and the decision on that label is open.

Who is in the test

  • Active MM. A HYPE MM on the event date with at least one post-only (ALO) fill in the two hours before the box starts (§4.1). 120,142 event × MM rows, 914 events, 2,132 MMs.
  • Accumulation A. On the MM’s 1-minute position path qt, rebuilt from its own fills, xt = s (qt − qt0) is the inventory built since the box start t0, with s = +1 when takers sell and −1 when they buy. A is the largest xt inside the box and t* is the first minute that reaches it.
  • Own rule. A is at least one of the MM’s own sigma (sig24), the peak level is at least one sigma away from its six-hour median, and its absorption-side maker fills exceed its opposite-side fills. For an MM with sig24 = 663 HYPE, the median in this population, it must build 663 HYPE. 25,081 rows.
  • Population rule. A is at or above the 75th percentile of A across the event’s active MMs, with the same fill condition. The threshold is 604 HYPE at the median event (392 at p25, 989 at p75). This rule adds large MMs whose accumulation is normal for them. 28,530 rows.
  • Accumulators. Rows that pass either rule: 35,612 rows, 914 events, 890 MMs. Shocked accumulators also clear the shock rule of §4.1 (|z| ≥ 3 on the box’s position change): 6,236 rows, 820 events, 568 MMs.

Column key and source

One row is an event × MM pair; events and MMs count distinct values. Every date, 2025-10-10 included. The per-cell row counts of each quote measure are lower because a row without a resting order in a window has no distance; they are in the source table. Source tables/unwind0917_population.csv, tables/unwind0917_window_changes.csv (columns n, events).

Speed classes, windows and equations
  • T60. Minutes after t* until xt first falls to 0.4 A (60% given back), on the 1-minute grid, capped at 360. Fast: T60 ≤ 10. Middle: 11 to 60. Slow: above 60 or never within 6 hours. The median T60 is 4 minutes for fast rows, 26 for middle and 360 (the cap) for slow. Fixed cuts rather than terciles, because a quarter of all rows never reach 60% within 6 hours (§12.3 uses the Exp9 cuts of 30 and 120 minutes on a different population).
  • Windows. All windows after the peak start at t*, the MM’s own peak minute, not at a point of the event:
    PRE2H = [t0 − 2 h, t0), the baseline, two hours before the box starts;
    UNW = [t*, t* + 2 h), two hours after the peak;
    H60 = [t*, t* + min(T60, 120) min), while the MM still holds more than 40% of A: a median 4 minutes for fast rows, 26 for middle, 120 for slow;
    M5 = [t*, t* + 5 min) and M15 = [t*, t* + 15 min), fixed clocks of the same length for every class.
  • Distances. Every minute the MM’s resting post-only and GTC orders are read at the minute instant. dside is the median over the window’s minutes of the closest order’s distance to that side’s best price, in bps of mid, 0 at the touch, positive behind it.
  • Skew. skew = dabsorption − dexit, so a positive skew means the exit-side quote is nearer the touch. The change is Δskew = skewwindow − skewPRE2H on the same row; “toward exit” is the share of rows with Δskew > 0.
  • Throughput. Exit fills / A = (exit-side maker + taker HYPE in UNW) / A; refills / A = absorption-side HYPE in UNW / A; net / A = the difference.
  • Markouts. mh = s (mid(t + h) − p) n for a fill of size n at price p, sign s = +1 for a buy; bps = 10,000 × Σmh / Σvolume over the class’s maker fills in the window and on the side (§4.1).

Column key and source

Volume-weighted markouts of maker fills in the window on the side; positive is money made by the MM. The 5- and 60-minute horizons are in the source table. The shocked fast class has $0.12bn of maker volume while held, so its cells are noisy. Source tables/unwind0917_markouts.csv.

  • Fast unwinders lean toward the exit the most, while they hold the position.
    While held, the fast class moves its skew +4.41 bps toward the exit and 80% of rows move that way; the slow class moves +0.56 bps. Among shocked accumulators it is +5.39 against +1.13.
  • The same order holds on an equal clock.
    Over the first 5 minutes after the peak the fast class moves +2.99 bps and the slow class −0.79: in those minutes the slow MMs are still absorbing and their exit quote moves away (+1.27 bps).
  • Two hours hide it.
    Over the two hours after the peak the fast class shows +0.00 bps and the slow class +0.55. A four-minute lean averaged with 116 minutes of level quoting is zero at the median. §12.3 found the same state dependence on the Exp9 shocks.
  • The lean is mostly the absorption-side quote stepping back.
    While held, the fast class moves its absorption-side quote +2.84 bps away and its exit-side quote −0.73 bps nearer; the exit side’s share of resting size rises by +0.059.
  • Nobody crosses to get out.
    The exit-side taker share changes by 0 at the median in every class and window, and exit-side taker fills are 0.00 of A at the median for fast accumulators (0.06 for shocked ones).
  • Speed is volume on both sides.
    Exit-side fills are 7.98, 2.99 and 0.50 times A for fast, middle and slow; absorption-side fills 6.61, 1.81 and 0.67. The fill mix barely leans: 54% of a fast MM’s own HYPE is on the exit side, against 48% for a slow one. Fast MMs place a median 39 exit-side orders per minute after the peak and cancel almost all of them; slow MMs place 7.5.
  • The ordering runs mostly between MMs.
    On the first 5 minutes the rank correlation of T60 with the lean is −0.53 across MMs and −0.04 inside an MM. Inside an MM the effect is weak but not absent: among the 115 MMs with at least three fast and three slow rows, the fast rows lean more in 68% of them, by a median +1.24 bps. Among shocked accumulators only 27 MMs qualify and the share is 48%.
  • Getting out costs the fast and middle classes.
    Exit-side maker fills over the two hours mark out at −9.5 (fast) and −13.5 bps (middle) at 30 minutes, while absorption-side fills after the peak make +13.8 and +19.8; the slow class’s exit fills make +7.2.

What this does not establish: the speed classes are defined on the outcome, so a class comparison is not the effect of a strategy chosen before the event, and a large two-sided flow shortens T60 mechanically for a given A. Quotes are read at the minute instant, while the median order in the ten inspected episodes lives 0.7 to 5.7 seconds, so distances describe the part of the book that survives a minute boundary. About 27% of rows fall on dates with holes in the order store (§4.1); restricted to covered dates the medians of Table 68 are unchanged within the bound in its key. Order-message rates exist only for rows with A ≥ 0.5 sig24. Record: analysis.md §47 to §49; code code/unwind0917_report_tables.py and code/unwind0917_section_12_5.py.

Earlier version of this section (2026-09-16): 25,705 own-rule rows, two-hour window, timing and speed classes

Superseded on 2026-09-17 by the version above. Its numbers are correct for the two-hour window on its population; the readings “fast and early MMs do not tilt at all” and “inside an MM, more tilt goes with a slower unwind” do not survive the windows that start at the peak.

On the 25,705 absorbers of §4.4, the fast and early MMs do not tilt their quotes at all while they unwind; the slow and late MMs tilt by about one basis point, by moving the absorption-side quote away rather than by bringing the exit-side quote in. No class crosses the spread to get out: the exit-side taker share is zero at the median before and during the unwind. The exit-side fills of every class but the slowest lose money over the next 30 to 120 minutes, and the absorption-side fills that continue after the peak make it.

Setup, definitions and equations
  • Rows. The 25,705 event × MM rows of §4.4 (accumulation A ≥ 1 sig24, level L ≥ 1 sig24, absorption-side maker fills above opposite-side fills), on all 914 events including 2025-10-10; the version without 2025-10-10 (25,561 rows) is in the source tables and moves the class medians of Table 76 by at most 0.21 bps.
  • Windows. PRE2H = [t0 − 2 h, t0); ACC = [t0, t*); UNW = [t*, t* + 2 h), where t* is the wallet's own absorption-side peak (§4.4).
  • Sides. SAME is the absorption side, OPP the exit side. Skew = SAME distance − OPP distance, so a positive skew means the exit-side order is nearer the touch.
  • Speed classes (T60). T60 is the number of minutes after t* until 60% of A is given back, on the 1-minute position grid, capped at 360 (never within 6 h). Fast: T60 ≤ 10 min (7,014 rows, 27%). Middle: 11 to 60 min (6,120, 24%). Slow: above 60 min or never (12,571, 49%; 26% of all rows never reach 60% within 6 h). Fixed cuts, not quantiles: T60 has no natural break and a quarter of rows are censored, so a tercile cut would fall at 197 minutes inside the censored mass. The 5 / 120 cuts are the sensitivity, in the source tables.
  • Timing classes. The §4.4 labels: early (half of A given back by the price extreme, 5,340), late holding more than half (16,510), late with the peak after the price extreme (3,855).
  • Quotes. 1-minute snapshots of the wallet's resting post-only and GTC limit orders. The touch is the market's best same-side level as of the minute. Best-level distance = median over the window's minutes with an order of the closest order's distance to the touch, in bps of mid, 0 at the touch. Size-weighted distance = resting-size-weighted mean distance over all order-minutes. Size = mean resting HYPE per minute, 0 in minutes with no order. The change is UNW − PRE2H for the same row; "toward exit" is the share of rows whose change has the sign that tilts toward getting out.
  • Markouts. For a fill of size n at price p with sign s (+1 buy, −1 sell), mh = s (mid(t + h) − p) n, from the stored columns of the grouped trade table, verified against a rebuild from the book within 0.03 bps on ordinary days and 0.41 bps on 2025-10-10. The table shows 10,000 × Σmh / Σvolume over all fills of the class in the window and on the side, maker and taker together.
  • Source. tables/unwind0915_skewmk_class_counts.csv, _quotes.csv, _markouts.csv, _within_mm.csv; 16 of 19 validation checks pass (row count, key uniqueness, 120 minutes per window, book staleness, mid-distance medians against the §4 population columns, fill USD against the §4.4 build).

Column key and source

Each cell holds the five quantiles across rows of the class, one per line, median third. The change row is the paired UNW − PRE2H difference over rows with both windows defined, with the share of rows whose change tilts toward the exit underneath. Distances in bps of mid to the market's best same-side level; sizes in HYPE per minute. Source tables/unwind0915_skewmk_quotes.csv, sample "every date".

Column key and source

Every fill of the class's wallets in the window (maker and taker together), on the absorption side and on the exit side; volume is the summed fill USD. A positive value means the fill made money by the horizon. Before-window fills reach into the event at the longer horizons, which is why the absorption side already loses in PRE2H. Source tables/unwind0915_skewmk_markouts.csv, sample "every date", role "all".

  • The classes differ in book shape before the event, not in tilt.
    Fast and early MMs quote both sides about 4.1 bps from the touch with 372 HYPE resting on the exit side; slow MMs sit 9.8 bps away with 47 HYPE. The median skew is zero in every class before the event.
  • Slow and late MMs tilt about one basis point toward the exit during the unwind; fast and early MMs do not tilt at all.
    The median paired change in the best-level skew is +1.14 bps for the slow class and +0.80 for late holders, against +0.00 for the fast class and +0.00 for early unwinders. The tilt comes from the absorption side moving away (+0.55 bps, slow), not from the exit side coming in (-0.24 bps).
  • Nobody crosses to get out.
    The exit-side taker share of the wallet's own volume is 0 at the median in every class, before and during the unwind; the paired change is 0.
  • Inside an MM, more tilt goes with a slower unwind.
    Among the 96 MMs with at least three fast and three slow rows, the own fast-unwind skew change minus the own slow-unwind skew change has a median of -0.77 bps, and the fast rows show the larger tilt in only 35% of them. Across MMs the rank correlation of T60 with the skew change is -0.13, pooled +0.08. This is the §12.4 result on a population three times larger: the exit lean does not buy speed.
  • The exit fills lose and the continued absorption fills gain.
    In the unwind window, exit-side fills mark out at -10.9 bps (fast) and -13.5 bps (late holders) at 30 minutes, while absorption-side fills made after the peak mark out at +11.1 and +18.3 bps. The price keeps moving in the surge direction after the wallet's own peak, so getting out costs and staying in pays over the next two hours. Only the slow class's exit fills come out ahead (+4.9 bps at 30 minutes, -3.5 at 120): they exit late enough that the move has run.
  • The accumulation itself is the expensive part.
    Absorption-side fills inside ACC mark out at -71.0 bps (early) to -53.5 bps (late holders) at 30 minutes; the exit-side fills made during the same window mark out at +92.3 and +78.4. Early unwinders take the largest hit per dollar absorbed and give the position back within minutes.

What this does not establish: the classes are defined on the outcome (T60, or the give-back at the price extreme), so a within-class markout is not the return to a strategy chosen before the event. The quote rows exist only for the 74% of rows on order-covered dates (§4.1). Sensitivity at the 5 / 120 cuts and with the 1-minute T60 rows dropped is in the source tables.
